Jennifer Lieber was taken into custody that night and brought to the Scott County Sheriff's Office. She offered little at the station, and investigators relied on the physical evidence, the phone recorded footage from earlier that evening, and the statements from the children to understand what had unfolded inside the home. According to the medical examiner, David Nanavik died from a single contact gunshot wound to the head. Puzzle pressed directly against him when it fired. Gunshot residue testing detected particles on Lieber's right hand, placing her close to the weapon when it discharged. Testing on David produced a negative result, though the medical examiner noted that a lack of residue does not rule out handling or firing a weapon. DNA from both Lieber and Nanavik was found on the grip of the weapon, while only David's DNA appeared on the cartridge still in the chamber, suggesting he had handled or loaded it at some point. But with no witnesses, inconclusive gunshot residue tests in a casing that failed to eject, the manner of death was ruled. was ruled undetermined. The forensic evidence could not say with certainty who pulled the trigger, a reality that left David's 10-year-old son without either parent in his life. Investigators also noted that Lieber never called 911 after the shooting, and the story she later gave, claiming she kicked the gun out of David's hand and it went off, did not match the physical evidence or the contact range wound documented by the medical examiner. Prosecutors argued that the escalating behavior captured in Jennifer's voice to text messages and the phone recorded footage, combined with the children's accounts of the night, demonstrated a pattern of volatility and intent. Jennifer Lieber would ultimately face a charge of second-degree murder with intent, and in January 2026, a jury found her guilty. On April 7, 2026, she was sentenced to 306 months in prison, 25 and a half years, for second-degree murder with intent. She was taken into custody immediately, and will serve her sentence at the Minnesota Correctional Facility in Shakopee. Cases like this take a tremendous amount of work to bring together. We spend weeks going through reports, reviewing footage, reading court filings, and organizing every detail into a clear, watchable story. There's a lot behind the scenes, the documents, the photos, the timelines, and we do our best to shape all of it into something engaging and easy to follow. We put a lot into these videos because we care about the work, and we care about telling these stories the right way. Thank you to our subscribers for helping make detailed reporting like this possible.
